# Scope and verification claims

This notebook verifies Phase 1 of `magnetofluidics_pinn` (`v0.1.6+`): a single
spherical particle carried by steady Stokes flow through a straight channel,
under a uniform magnetic field. It checks that against the one case with a
closed-form solution, axisymmetric Hagen–Poiseuille
flow [@happel1983low; @leal2007advanced], and it does so twice — once for
each of the two ways the package can write the axisymmetric residual. The
`"standard"` form keeps the momentum and continuity equations exactly as
written, with their native $1/r$ and $1/r^2$ terms, which means collocation
points have to stay off the symmetry axis. The `"r_weighted"` form
multiplies those same equations through by $r$ or $r^2$, which removes the
singularity algebraically and lets points be drawn flush against the axis —
at a cost that [
`physics.fluid_residuals`](../magnetofluidics_pinn/physics/fluid_residuals.py)'s
own documentation is candid about, and that this notebook measures directly
rather than takes on faith. Training both formulations under otherwise
identical conditions, and putting the same battery of checks to each, is
how it decides whether that trade is worth making.

Three package components are exercised throughout: the governing-equation
residual (`physics.fluid_residuals.stokes_residual`), the trained network's
hard-constrained architecture
(`networks.constraints.apply_hard_wall_constraint` [@lu2021physics]), and
the particle-trajectory integrator (`trajectory.integrate_trajectory`).

## What this notebook does not verify

Phase 2 (particle swarms, non-uniform fields) and Phase 3 (Navier–Stokes,
bifurcated geometry) stay out of scope:
`boundary_conditions.magnetic_field_bc.gradient_field` and
`biot_savart_field`, and `geometry.build_bifurcation_domain`, are
unimplemented in this release and are never called here. The Faxén-law
finite-size correction [@faxen1922widerstand; @kim2005microhydrodynamics] is
checked only against its own closed-form prediction for this flow, not
against an independent finite-size hydrodynamics reference. The magnetic
field stays uniform throughout — `integrate_trajectory` rejects anything
else by design — under which the dipole force vanishes
identically [@abbott2020magnetic].

@tbl-preview previews every claim this notebook makes, before any of the
expensive computation runs. Each row fills in as its own section executes,
and the completed table is repeated at the end, in @sec-summary. Every
check accumulates into `verification_checks` as it happens, so nothing here
gets graded twice and nothing gets skipped silently.

# Reference problem and analytical solution

## Governing equations

In dimensionless axisymmetric cylindrical coordinates $(r^*, z^*)$, the standard
Stokes momentum and continuity equations read:
$$-\pdv{p^*}{r^*} + \laplacian u_r^* - \frac{u_r^*}{r^{*2}} = 0, \qquad
-\pdv{p^*}{z^*} + \laplacian u_z^* = 0, \qquad
\frac{1}{r^*}\pdv{ (r^* u_r^*)}{r^*} + \pdv{u_z^*}{z^*} = 0.$$

Driven by a parabolic inlet profile and a fixed outlet gauge pressure, this
system has the classical closed-form solution
$$u_r^*(r^*, z^*) = 0, \qquad
u_z^*(r^*, z^*) = u_\text{peak}^*\left (1 - \left (\frac{r^*}{R^*}\right)^2\right), \qquad
\pdv{p^*}{z^*} = -\frac{4 u_\text{peak}^*}{R^{*2}}.$$
with the last relation following from substituting $u_z^*$ into the
$z$-momentum equation above. Integrating the parabolic profile over a
cross-section gives the reference volumetric flow rate
$$Q_\text{ref}^* = \int_0^{R^*} u_z^*(r^*)\, 2\pi r^*\, dr^* = \frac{\pi R^{*2} u_\text{peak}^*}{2}.$$

These three closed forms —
[
`hagen_poiseuille_velocity_field`](../magnetofluidics_pinn/verification/analytical.py),
[
`analytical_pressure_gradient`](../magnetofluidics_pinn/verification/analytical.py),
and
[
`poiseuille_reference_flow_rate`](../magnetofluidics_pinn/physics/conservation.py) —
are every quantitative reference this notebook compares against.

## Configuration and scales

```{python}
#| label: reference-problem
radius = 7.5e-4             # 750µm
reference_velocity =1.0e-3  # 1 mm/s
length = 4.0 * radius       # 3 mm
dynamic_viscosity = 1e-3    # 1 mPa·s
density = 1.0e3             # 1000 kg/m^3

n_interior_points: int = 5_000  #  Number of interior collocation points per Adam epoch
n_boundary_points: int = 1_000   # Number of boundary collocation points per Adam epoch.
n_epochs = 250
lbfgs_n_interior_points: int = 2_000
lbfgs_n_boundary_points: int = 500
lbfgs_rounds = 5
lbfgs_iterations_per_round = 400
log_every = int(n_epochs / 5)

# The dimensionless inlet centerline velocity: `FluidConfig.reference_velocity`
# is, by construction of `compute_scales`, the physical velocity that maps to
# exactly 1.0, matching `training.trainer`'s own gauge choice.
PEAK_VELOCITY = 1.0
REFERENCE_PRESSURE = 0.0

fluid_config = mfp.FluidConfig(
    regime="stokes", dynamic_viscosity=dynamic_viscosity, density=density,
)
domain_config = mfp.DomainConfig(kind="channel", length=length, 
                                 radius=radius, u_max=reference_velocity,
                                 fluid=fluid_config)
field_config = mfp.MagneticFieldConfig(source="uniform", magnitude=1.0e-2, orientation=(1.0, 0.0))
particle_config = mfp.ParticleConfig(radius=10.0e-6, magnetic_moment=(1.0e-11, 0.0))

physical_domain = mfp.build_channel_domain(domain_config)
scales = mfp.compute_scales(domain_config, field_config)
domain = mfp.nondimensionalize_domain(physical_domain, scales)

thresholds = mfp.default_thresholds(dtype=DTYPE, peak_velocity=PEAK_VELOCITY)

pd.Series({"domain.radius": domain.radius, "domain.length": domain.length,
           "scales.length [m]": scales.length, "scales.velocity [m/s]": scales.velocity,
           "scales.pressure [Pa]": scales.pressure})
```

Setting the reference length equal to the channel radius fixes the
dimensionless radius at exactly $R^*=$ `{python} f"{domain.radius:.3e}"`, so
the dimensionless length, $L^*=$ `{python} f"{domain.length:.3e}"`, is just
the physical aspect ratio, `{python} f"{length / radius:.1f}"`. That is the
whole purpose of this nondimensionalization: a physical radius of
`{python} f"{radius:.3e}"` m and a viscous pressure scale of
`{python} f"{scales.pressure:.3e}"` Pa both land on order-unity numbers,
which is what a gradient-based optimizer conditions on well ---the
alternative, training directly against raw SI values spanning several
decades, is what `compute_scales` exists to avoid.

```{python}
#| label: reference-quantities
reference_flow_rate = mfp.poiseuille_reference_flow_rate(domain.radius, PEAK_VELOCITY)
reference_pressure_gradient = mfp.analytical_pressure_gradient(domain.radius, PEAK_VELOCITY)

pd.Series({"Q_ref* (analytical)": reference_flow_rate, "dp*/dz* (analytical)": reference_pressure_gradient})
```

Under $R^*=1$ and $u_\text{peak}^*=1$, these reduce to exact constants:
$Q_\text{ref}^*=\pi/2$ and $\pdv{p^*}{z^*}=-4$, matching the
`{python} f"{reference_flow_rate:.3e}"` and
`{python} f"{reference_pressure_gradient:.3e}"` printed above. The negative
sign on the pressure gradient is not incidental — pressure has to fall from
inlet to outlet for the flow to be driven forward at all. Both quantities
recur throughout the rest of this notebook as the fixed targets every
trained-network metric in @sec-independent-verification is measured
against.

# Exact differential-operator verification {#sec-exact-residual}

Evaluating `stokes_residual` on the closed-form solution isolates the
residual formula from any question about network training: on an
independent grid, disjoint from every seed used later for training or
held-out evaluation, the residual should sit at machine precision. A
convenient property of this particular flow makes that especially clean —
because $u_r^*\equiv0$ identically, the standard form's singular
$1/r^{*2}$ term is multiplied by an operand that is exactly zero in
floating point, so unlike a trained network, where a small numerical
$u_r^*$ gets amplified as $r\to0$, this grid needs no clearance around the
axis. A tiny floor (`1e-8`) on $r^*$ is kept only to stop an unlucky exact
zero from tripping the standard form's own $r>0$ guard.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-exact-residual
#| tbl-cap: "Exact Stokes residual of the closed-form solution, on an independent grid."
EXACT_GRID_SEED = RANDOM_SEED + 1000  # independent of every training/held-out seed below
N_EXACT_GRID_POINTS = 20_000

exact_grid_generator = torch.Generator(device=DEVICE).manual_seed(EXACT_GRID_SEED)
exact_r = (domain.radius * torch.rand(
    N_EXACT_GRID_POINTS, 1, generator=exact_grid_generator, device=DEVICE, dtype=DTYPE
)).clamp_min(1.0e-8)
exact_z = domain.length * torch.rand(
    N_EXACT_GRID_POINTS, 1, generator=exact_grid_generator, device=DEVICE, dtype=DTYPE
)
exact_coordinates = torch.cat([exact_r, exact_z], dim=1).requires_grad_(True)


def analytical_network(coordinates: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Closed-form Hagen-Poiseuille field, exposed with the trained-net_std calling convention."""
    return mfp.hagen_poiseuille_velocity_field(coordinates, domain, PEAK_VELOCITY, REFERENCE_PRESSURE)


exact_residual = mfp.stokes_residual(analytical_network, exact_coordinates, fluid_config, residual_form="standard")
exact_residual_summary = mfp.summarize_residual(exact_residual, ("momentum_r", "momentum_z", "continuity"))
exact_residual_summary
```

Every component sits at
`{python} f"{exact_residual_summary.loc['total', 'max_abs']:.3e}"` or
below ---for `float32`, that is floating-point noise, not a genuine equation
violation. Because $u_r^*\equiv0$, the $r$-momentum equation never gets the
chance to amplify truncation error the way it would near a network's
approximate zero, and the $z$-momentum residual reduces to
$-\pdv{p^*}{z^*}+\laplacian u_z^*$ evaluated on two polynomials whose
derivatives autograd computes exactly. What this table certifies is
narrower than "the flow is right": it certifies that `stokes_residual`'s
implementation of the governing equations and
`hagen_poiseuille_velocity_field`'s implementation of the solution agree
with each other to machine precision. Every nonzero residual reported
later in this notebook is therefore attributable to the network being
trained, never to a mismatch between the physics code and the target it is
trained against.

```{python}
#| label: check-exact-residual
verification_checks = verification_checks + (
    mfp.evaluate_check(
        "Exact interior residual",
        "Stokes residual of the closed-form solution on an independent grid",
        exact_residual_summary.loc["total", "max_abs"], thresholds.exact_residual_tolerance, "<=",
    ),
)
mfp.render_verification_table((verification_checks[-1],))
```

The standard form needs $r^*>0$ to stay well-defined, which is precisely
why the r-weighted form exists: multiplying the equations through by $r$
or $r^2$ removes the singularity algebraically, so the symmetry axis
itself becomes an admissible collocation point. That claim is worth
checking before training enters the picture, on the same closed-form
solution, with the axis included this time rather than floored away from.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-exact-residual-r-weighted
#| tbl-cap: "Exact Stokes residual of the closed-form solution under the r-weighted form, with the axis itself included."
exact_r_weighted_radial = torch.cat(
    [
        torch.zeros(1, 1, device=DEVICE, dtype=DTYPE),
        domain.radius * torch.rand(
            N_EXACT_GRID_POINTS - 1, 1, generator=exact_grid_generator, device=DEVICE, dtype=DTYPE
        ),
    ],
    dim=0,
)
exact_r_weighted_axial = domain.length * torch.rand(
    N_EXACT_GRID_POINTS, 1, generator=exact_grid_generator, device=DEVICE, dtype=DTYPE
)
exact_coordinates_r_weighted = torch.cat(
    [exact_r_weighted_radial, exact_r_weighted_axial], dim=1
).requires_grad_(True)

exact_residual_r_weighted = mfp.stokes_residual(
    analytical_network, exact_coordinates_r_weighted, fluid_config, residual_form="r_weighted"
)
exact_residual_summary_r_weighted = mfp.summarize_residual(
    exact_residual_r_weighted, ("momentum_r", "momentum_z", "continuity")
)
exact_residual_summary_r_weighted
```

Every component is again at machine precision,
`{python} f"{exact_residual_summary_r_weighted.loc['total', 'max_abs']:.3e}"`
at most, including the row evaluated exactly at $r^*=0$. That is the
entire benefit the r-weighted form offers at this stage of the
notebook: it covers the one point the standard form cannot touch, and it
does so without any loss of exactness on the analytical solution. What it
costs is a separate question, one that only shows up once a network has to
learn from the weighted residual rather than simply have it evaluated —
@sec-comparison returns to it once both networks are trained.

```{python}
#| label: check-exact_residual_summary_r_weighted
verification_checks = verification_checks + (
    mfp.evaluate_check(
        "Exact interior residual",
        "Stokes residual of the closed-form solution on an independent grid",
        exact_residual_summary_r_weighted.loc["total", "max_abs"], thresholds.exact_residual_tolerance, "<=",
    ),
)
mfp.render_verification_table((verification_checks[-1],))
```

# Structural boundary/regularity verification {#sec-structural}

`apply_hard_wall_constraint` claims to enforce axis and wall regularity
structurally — for every parameter value, not just after
training [@lu2021physics]. The only way to actually test that claim is to
probe a freshly initialized, untrained network: if the conditions hold
before a single gradient step, they hold by construction, not by
coincidence of training. Nothing about this check depends on which
residual form a network will later be trained under, since the wrapper's
algebra never references `residual_form` at all, so a single untrained
network stands in for both formulations here.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-structural
#| tbl-cap: "Structural axis/wall regularity, probed on an untrained net_std."
base_training_config=mfp.TrainingConfig(random_seed=RANDOM_SEED, 
                                        device=str(DEVICE),
                                        verbose=True,log_every=log_every)
untrained_net_std = mfp.apply_hard_wall_constraint(
    mfp.build_mlp(n_inputs=2, n_outputs=3, hidden_layers=(32, 32, 32), 
                  training_config=base_training_config,
                  activation="tanh"),
    domain,
)
structural_metrics = mfp.evaluate_structural_constraints(
    untrained_net_std, domain, n_probe_points=2_000, random_seed=EXACT_GRID_SEED + 1,
)
pd.Series(structural_metrics)
```

All five probes read `{python} f"{max(structural_metrics.values()):.3e}"`
or smaller, on a network whose weights are still Xavier-random — no
training has happened yet. That is the entire point of a structural
constraint: $u_r (0,z)=u_r (R,z)=u_z (R,z)=0$ and the two derivative
conditions hold not because gradient descent found weights that satisfy
them, but because the reparametrization — multiplying the raw network's
output by $(r/R)(1- (r/R)^2)$ for $u_r$ and $1- (r/R)^2$ for $u_z$ — forces
both to vanish identically at $r=0$ and $r=R$ for any input at all. A
nonzero value here would point to a bug in the wrapper's algebra, not an
undertrained model; every probe sitting at floating-point noise confirms
the wrapper does exactly what its docstring claims.

```{python}
#| label: check-structural
verification_checks = verification_checks + (
    mfp.evaluate_check(
        "Structural regularity",
        "Axis/wall hard-constraint probe on an untrained net_std",
        max(structural_metrics.values()), thresholds.structural_tolerance, "<=",
    ),
)
mfp.render_verification_table((verification_checks[-1],))
```

# PINN training {#sec-training}

Both formulations get the same architecture — the same three-layer,
thirty-two-unit-wide `tanh` network, wrapped by the same hard-wall
constraint — trained for the same number of epochs under the same loss
weights. The only differences are the residual formula itself and, for
the r-weighted run, an `axis_clearance_fraction` of zero: the entire
reason to weight the residual by $r$ or $r^2$ is to make the axis safe to
sample, so leaving the usual clearance in place would waste the one thing
that formulation buys.

::: {.callout-warning title="Reduced, notebook-scale recipe"}
The configuration below trains for `{python} f"{n_epochs:,d}"` Adam epochs
and `{python} f"{lbfgs_rounds:d}"` rounds of
`{python} f"{lbfgs_iterations_per_round:,d}"` L-BFGS iterations each — well
short of `TrainingConfig()`'s defaults (20 000 epochs, four rounds of five
hundred iterations), so this notebook renders in minutes rather than
hours. Every loss weight stays at its package default. The accuracy the
package's own documentation reports assumes the full recipe; every number
measured below should be read with that in mind.
:::

```{python}
#| label: training-config
training_config_standard = mfp.TrainingConfig(
    n_interior_points=n_interior_points, n_boundary_points=n_boundary_points,
    n_epochs=n_epochs, random_seed=RANDOM_SEED, device=str(DEVICE),
    use_lbfgs_refinement=True,
    lbfgs_n_interior_points=lbfgs_n_interior_points,
    lbfgs_n_boundary_points=lbfgs_n_boundary_points,
    lbfgs_rounds=lbfgs_rounds,
    lbfgs_iterations_per_round=lbfgs_iterations_per_round,
    residual_form="standard",
    verbose=True, log_every=log_every
)
training_config_standard
training_config_r_weighted = mfp.TrainingConfig(
    n_interior_points=n_interior_points, n_boundary_points=n_boundary_points,
    n_epochs=n_epochs, random_seed=RANDOM_SEED + 1, device=str(DEVICE),
    use_lbfgs_refinement=True,
    lbfgs_n_interior_points=lbfgs_n_interior_points,
    lbfgs_n_boundary_points=lbfgs_n_boundary_points,
    lbfgs_rounds=lbfgs_rounds, lbfgs_iterations_per_round=lbfgs_iterations_per_round,
    residual_form="r_weighted", axis_clearance_fraction=0.0,
    verbose=True, log_every=log_every
)
training_config_r_weighted
```

```{python}
#| label: train
network_standard = mfp.apply_hard_wall_constraint(
    mfp.build_mlp(n_inputs=2, n_outputs=3, hidden_layers=(32, 32, 32),
                  training_config = training_config_standard, 
                  activation="tanh",),
    domain,
)
network_r_weighted = mfp.apply_hard_wall_constraint(
    mfp.build_mlp(n_inputs=2, n_outputs=3, hidden_layers=(32, 32, 32), 
                  training_config = training_config_r_weighted, 
                  activation="tanh",),
    domain,
)

training_start = time.perf_counter()
trained_network_standard, training_history_standard = mfp.train(
    network=network_standard, domain=domain, fluid_config=fluid_config, field_config=field_config,
    training_config=training_config_standard, 
)
print(f"\nStandard formulation trained in {time.perf_counter() - training_start:.1f} s")
training_history_standard.print_summary()

training_start = time.perf_counter()
trained_network_r_weighted, training_history_r_weighted = mfp.train(
    network=network_r_weighted, domain=domain, fluid_config=fluid_config, field_config=field_config,
    training_config=training_config_r_weighted,
)
print(f"r-weighted formulation trained in {time.perf_counter() - training_start:.1f} s")
training_history_r_weighted.print_summary()
```

```{python}
#| label: training-reduction
initial_total_loss = training_history_standard.adam.total[0]
final_total_loss_standard = (training_history_standard.lbfgs.total or training_history_standard.adam.total)[-1]
final_total_loss_r_weighted = (training_history_r_weighted.lbfgs.total or training_history_r_weighted.adam.total)[-1]
total_loss_reduction = initial_total_loss / max(final_total_loss_standard, 1.0e-15)
```

The standard run's composite loss falls from
`{python} f"{initial_total_loss:.3e}"` to
`{python} f"{final_total_loss_standard:.3e}"`, a
`{python} f"{total_loss_reduction:.1f}"`-fold reduction; the r-weighted run
ends at `{python} f"{final_total_loss_r_weighted:.3e}"`. Reading anything
into that particular comparison would be premature — @sec-comparison
explains why once both networks have been measured against the same
physical checks, not just against their own training objectives. What the
two runs do agree on is the shape of convergence, and it is the shape
documented elsewhere in the PINN
literature [@krishnapriyan2021characterizing; @wang2021understanding]: the
boundary terms (wall, inlet, outlet) settle within the first few hundred
Adam epochs, since a small network satisfies a handful of Dirichlet
conditions without much trouble, while the interior residual and the
global conservation term keep falling well into the L-BFGS phase.

```{python}
#| label: fig-training-history-standard
#| fig-cap: "Adam + L-BFGS loss convergence, standard formulation, by component."
mfp.plot_training_history(training_history_standard)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-training-history-r-weighted
#| fig-cap: "Adam + L-BFGS loss convergence, r-weighted formulation, by component."
mfp.plot_training_history(training_history_r_weighted)
```

The two convergence patterns are qualitatively the same, which is worth
noting before anything else: the vertical dashed line marks the
Adam-to-L-BFGS handoff in both figures, the boundary panels (wall, inlet,
outlet) have already flattened by that point in both, and the interior
residual panels keep bending downward across it in both, which is
L-BFGS's curvature-aware step doing what Adam's first-order updates
plateau on. Neither formulation looks pathological on its own terms.
What the two panels cannot show is the one thing that actually
distinguishes them — each is plotted against its own residual definition,
so a lower r-weighted curve does not mean a smaller physical error; it
may just mean a smaller number, for reasons @sec-comparison makes precise.
Under the reduced recipe here, expect the bend near the Adam/L-BFGS
handoff to still be in progress when training stops, in both cases — a
training-budget observation, not a formulation concern. Loss convergence
is itself a training diagnostic, not a verification result: a low
training loss does not by itself establish physical accuracy against an
independent reference, which is why @sec-independent-verification exists
as a separate step, and @sec-comparison as another one after it.

# Independent hydrodynamic verification {#sec-independent-verification}

Every metric below is computed by
[`verification.metrics`](../magnetofluidics_pinn/verification/metrics.py)
against data the training loop never directly optimizes as a single
scalar: profiles, global and pointwise error fields, the flow-rate curve,
and a held-out residual batch drawn with its own independent seed. This
section covers the standard formulation, the one Phase 1 uses by default;
@sec-comparison repeats the same measurements for the r-weighted network
and reads the two side by side.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-profile-invariance
#| tbl-cap: "Predicted axial-velocity profile error and invariance across three axial stations."
Z_STATIONS = (0.1 * domain.length, 0.5 * domain.length, 0.9 * domain.length)
RADIAL_GRID = torch.linspace(0.0, domain.radius, 200, device=DEVICE, dtype=DTYPE)
AXIAL_GRID = torch.linspace(0.0, domain.length, 200, device=DEVICE, dtype=DTYPE)

profile_evaluation = mfp.evaluate_velocity_profiles(trained_network_standard, domain, Z_STATIONS, RADIAL_GRID, PEAK_VELOCITY)
profile_invariance = mfp.compute_profile_invariance(profile_evaluation)
profile_invariance
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-profile-invariance-r
#| tbl-cap: "Predicted axial-velocity profile error and invariance across three axial stations for r-weighted residual."
profile_evaluation_r = mfp.evaluate_velocity_profiles(trained_network_r_weighted, domain, Z_STATIONS, RADIAL_GRID, PEAK_VELOCITY)
profile_invariance_r = mfp.compute_profile_invariance(profile_evaluation_r)
profile_invariance_r
```

The two error columns bound the same gap from different angles. Against
the analytical curve, the worst station reaches
`{python} f"{profile_invariance['max_abs_error_vs_analytical'].max():.3e}"`;
against the other stations' own average, independent of the analytical
target, the worst deviation is
`{python} f"{profile_invariance['max_abs_deviation_from_mean_profile'].max():.3e}"`.
A large first number with a small second one would mean the network
learned a consistent, $z$-independent profile that is simply the wrong
shape; a large second number would mean it predicts a different profile
at every station and has not learned the flow's steadiness at all — a
failure no amount of matching the analytical curve at any one station
would fix. Hagen–Poiseuille flow has no $z$-dependence anywhere in the
channel, so both numbers should shrink together as training improves.

```{python}
#| label: global-pointwise-error
global_l2_error = mfp.compute_global_l2_error(trained_network_standard, domain, RADIAL_GRID, AXIAL_GRID, PEAK_VELOCITY)
max_pointwise_error = mfp.compute_max_pointwise_error(trained_network_standard, domain, RADIAL_GRID, AXIAL_GRID, PEAK_VELOCITY)
pd.Series({"Global relative L2 error": global_l2_error, "Max pointwise velocity error": max_pointwise_error})
```

The global relative $L^2$ error is `{python} f"{global_l2_error:.3e}"`
against a `{python} f"{thresholds.global_l2_tolerance:.3e}"` budget; the
maximum pointwise error is `{python} f"{max_pointwise_error:.3e}"` against
`{python} f"{thresholds.max_pointwise_tolerance:.3e}"`. The two answer
different questions. $L^2$ averages the squared error over the whole
$(r,z)$ grid, so it stays small even with a poorly fit boundary layer as
long as most of the bulk is accurate, while the pointwise maximum is
exactly the statistic that would catch that failure mode. Seeing the
pointwise error several times larger than the (already squared, so
naturally smaller-looking) $L^2$ figure is normal on its own; it would
only be a concern if it stayed large once the leakage and flow-rate checks
below also settled.

```{python}
#| label: leakage
leakage_metrics = mfp.compute_radial_leakage(profile_evaluation, PEAK_VELOCITY)
pd.Series(leakage_metrics)
```

Radial leakage — the network's predicted $u_r$, which the analytical
solution sets to exactly zero everywhere — peaks at
`{python} f"{leakage_metrics['max_abs_radial_leakage']:.3e}"`, or
`{python} f"{leakage_metrics['normalized_radial_leakage']:.3e}"` of the
centerline velocity, against a
`{python} f"{thresholds.normalized_leakage_tolerance:.3e}"` budget. This is
not a free-standing statistic: by the axisymmetric continuity equation,
$\pdv{Q}{z}=-2\pi R\, u_r (R,z)$, so any nonzero $u_r$ at the wall directly
measures how fast mass conservation is being violated along the
channel — the flow-rate deviation checked next is this same leakage,
integrated.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-flow-rate
#| tbl-cap: "Predicted volumetric flow rate Q(z) versus the analytical reference."
N_FLOW_RATE_QUADRATURE_POINTS = 64
flow_rate_curve = mfp.compute_flow_rate_curve(trained_network_standard, domain, AXIAL_GRID, n_quadrature_points=N_FLOW_RATE_QUADRATURE_POINTS)
flow_rate_errors = mfp.compute_flow_rate_errors(flow_rate_curve, reference_flow_rate)
pd.Series(flow_rate_errors)
```

$Q (z)$ deviates from $Q_\text{ref}^*$ by up to
`{python} f"{flow_rate_errors['max_relative_flow_rate_error']:.3e}"` in
relative terms (span across stations:
`{python} f"{flow_rate_errors['flow_rate_span']:.3e}"`, standard
deviation: `{python} f"{flow_rate_errors['flow_rate_std']:.3e}"`), against
a `{python} f"{thresholds.flow_rate_relative_tolerance:.3e}"` budget.
`axial_flow_rate` integrates the network's own predicted $u_z$ across each
cross-section, so this is a macroscopic, physically meaningful check
rather than the pointwise continuity residual `stokes_residual` already
enforces as a soft loss term — a network can satisfy that pointwise
residual well almost everywhere and still accumulate a biased flow-rate
drift along $z$, which is exactly the failure mode
`conservation_loss_weight`'s training-time term, and this check, are
designed to catch.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-pressure-gradient
#| tbl-cap: "Fitted versus analytical axial pressure gradient."
pressure_gradient_metrics = mfp.compute_pressure_gradient_error(
    trained_network_standard, domain, PEAK_VELOCITY, n_axial_points=100
)
pd.Series(pressure_gradient_metrics)
```

The fitted axial pressure gradient is
`{python} f"{pressure_gradient_metrics['predicted_pressure_gradient']:.3e}"`,
against the analytical
`{python} f"{pressure_gradient_metrics['analytical_pressure_gradient']:.3e}"`
— a relative error of
`{python} f"{pressure_gradient_metrics['relative_error']:.3e}"` against a
`{python} f"{thresholds.pressure_gradient_relative_tolerance:.3e}"` budget.
Because Stokes pressure is only defined up to an additive constant, only
the slope of $p^*(z^*)$ carries physical information — a network could in
principle predict an arbitrary constant offset and still be correct, which
is why this check compares gradients rather than raw pressure values, and
why the fitted intercept
(`{python} f"{pressure_gradient_metrics['fitted_intercept']:.3e}"`) is
reported separately rather than folded into the error.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-held-out-residual
#| tbl-cap: "Stokes residual on a held-out collocation batch, independent of every training-time seed."
N_HELD_OUT_POINTS = 5_000
held_out_residual = mfp.evaluate_held_out_residual(
    trained_network_standard, domain, fluid_config, random_seed=EXACT_GRID_SEED + 2, n_points=N_HELD_OUT_POINTS,
    residual_form=training_config_standard.residual_form,
    axis_clearance_fraction=training_config_standard.axis_clearance_fraction,
)
held_out_residual
```

On a `{python} f"{N_HELD_OUT_POINTS:,d}"`-point batch drawn under the same
volume-uniform measure training uses but with a seed that never appears
anywhere in `training_config_standard`, the residual RMS is
`{python} f"{held_out_residual.loc['total', 'rms']:.3e}"` (max:
`{python} f"{held_out_residual.loc['total', 'max_abs']:.3e}"`), against a
`{python} f"{thresholds.held_out_residual_tolerance:.3e}"` budget. This is
the check most directly analogous to a held-out test set in ordinary
machine learning: every other metric in this section is a downstream,
physically interpretable consequence of the PDE residual — a badly-fit
residual eventually shows up as leakage, flow-rate drift, or profile
inconsistency — while this one asks the equation-satisfaction question
directly, on points the optimizer's own batches never happened to
include.

```{python}
#| label: check-independent-verification
verification_checks = verification_checks + (
    mfp.evaluate_check(
        "Global relative L2 error",
        "Relative L2 error of the predicted velocity against the analytical profile",
        global_l2_error, thresholds.global_l2_tolerance, "<=",
    ),
    mfp.evaluate_check(
        "Max pointwise velocity error",
        "Largest pointwise velocity deviation from the analytical profile",
        max_pointwise_error, thresholds.max_pointwise_tolerance, "<=",
    ),
    mfp.evaluate_check(
        "Profile invariance",
        "Consistency of the predicted u_z(r) profile across axial stations",
        profile_invariance["max_abs_deviation_from_mean_profile"].max(), thresholds.max_velocity_invariant_tolerance, "<=",
    ),
    mfp.evaluate_check(
        "Radial leakage",
        "Normalized max |u_r|, relative to the centerline velocity",
        leakage_metrics["normalized_radial_leakage"], thresholds.normalized_leakage_tolerance, "<=",
    ),
    mfp.evaluate_check(
        "Flow-rate conservation",
        "Relative error of Q(z) against the analytical reference flow rate",
        flow_rate_errors["max_relative_flow_rate_error"], thresholds.flow_rate_relative_tolerance, "<=",
    ),
    mfp.evaluate_check(
        "Pressure-gradient fit",
        "Relative error of the fitted dp/dz against the analytical value",
        pressure_gradient_metrics["relative_error"], thresholds.pressure_gradient_relative_tolerance, "<=",
    ),
    mfp.evaluate_check(
        "Held-out PDE residual",
        "Stokes residual RMS on a fresh, independent collocation batch",
        held_out_residual.loc["total", "rms"], thresholds.held_out_residual_tolerance, "<=",
    ),
)
mfp.render_verification_table(verification_checks[-7:])
```

Each row above pairs one measured value from this section with its own
calibratable threshold from `thresholds`; the metric-by-metric discussion
above already covers what each one means physically. @sec-summary
revisits the aggregate pass/fail pattern once every remaining check has
run.

# Visualization

Each panel below renders a metric already computed above, for the
standard formulation — nothing here is recomputed from scratch. A few
small diagnostics (which station and radial fraction carry the largest
deviation, which end of a curve's sign or magnitude dominates) are
computed alongside each figure purely to ground its discussion in the
actual data, not to introduce a new metric.

```{python}
#| label: fig-velocity-profiles
#| fig-cap: "Predicted axial-velocity profiles at three axial stations, against the analytical profile."
mfp.plot_velocity_profile_comparison(profile_evaluation)
```

```{python}
#| label: profile-error-location
profile_error_tensor = (profile_evaluation.predicted_uz - profile_evaluation.analytical_uz.unsqueeze(0)).abs()
n_radial_points = profile_error_tensor.shape[1]
worst_profile_flat_index = int(profile_error_tensor.argmax())
worst_profile_station_index, worst_profile_radial_index = divmod(worst_profile_flat_index, n_radial_points)
worst_profile_station = Z_STATIONS[worst_profile_station_index]
worst_profile_radial_fraction = (profile_evaluation.radial_grid[worst_profile_radial_index] / domain.radius).item()
worst_profile_location = (
    "close to the channel wall, where the (1 - (r/R)^2) shaping factor most compresses the raw "
    "network's degrees of freedom"
    if worst_profile_radial_fraction > 0.7
    else "near the symmetry axis"
    if worst_profile_radial_fraction < 0.3
    else "in the channel's bulk, away from either the axis or the wall"
)
```

The largest single-point deviation across the three curves above occurs at
$z^*=$ `{python} f"{worst_profile_station:.3e}"`, at
$r/R=$ `{python} f"{worst_profile_radial_fraction:.2f}"` —
`{python} worst_profile_location`. A network still short of convergence
typically struggles with the boundary layer's curvature before it
struggles with the gentler curvature near the axis, since the hard-wall
constraint already fixes the value at $r=R$ exactly but says nothing about
how steeply the profile has to fall to reach it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-profile-error
#| fig-cap: "Axial-velocity profile error against the analytical solution."
mfp.plot_profile_error(profile_evaluation)
```

Reading @fig-profile-error alongside @fig-velocity-profiles: if a curve
above sits on one side of zero rather than crossing it, the network is
systematically over- or under-predicting velocity at that station rather
than merely noisy around the right answer — worth checking against the
sign of the flow-rate deviation discussed after @fig-flow-rate-deviation,
since a one-sided velocity error is exactly what produces a one-signed
flow-rate bias.

```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-leakage
#| fig-cap: "Predicted radial velocity (leakage) across the domain — ideally identically zero."
mfp.plot_radial_leakage(profile_evaluation)
```

```{python}
#| label: leakage-location
leakage_worst_flat_index = int(profile_evaluation.predicted_ur.abs().argmax())
leakage_worst_station_index, leakage_worst_radial_index = divmod(leakage_worst_flat_index, n_radial_points)
leakage_worst_station = Z_STATIONS[leakage_worst_station_index]
leakage_worst_radial_fraction = (profile_evaluation.radial_grid[leakage_worst_radial_index] / domain.radius).item()
```

Every curve above is pinned to exactly zero at both $r=0$ and $r=R$ — the
hard-wall constraint forces $u_r$ to vanish at both endpoints by
construction, for any network weights, so leakage can only appear in the
interior of the radial domain, never at the curve's own endpoints. The
worst point recorded here sits at
$r/R=$ `{python} f"{leakage_worst_radial_fraction:.2f}"`,
$z^*=$ `{python} f"{leakage_worst_station:.3e}"` — away from the two
structurally exact endpoints, exactly where this diagnostic can tell us
something the wrapper does not already guarantee.

```{python}
#| label: fig-flow-rate-deviation
#| fig-cap: "Deviation of the predicted flow rate Q(z) from its analytical reference."
mfp.plot_flow_rate_deviation(AXIAL_GRID, flow_rate_curve, reference_flow_rate)
```

```{python}
#| label: flow-rate-sign
flow_rate_deviation_curve = flow_rate_curve.detach() - reference_flow_rate
flow_rate_deviation_constant_sign = bool((flow_rate_deviation_curve > 0).all() or (flow_rate_deviation_curve < 0).all())
flow_rate_deviation_summary = (
    f"stays {'above' if flow_rate_deviation_curve.mean() > 0 else 'below'} the reference value everywhere"
    if flow_rate_deviation_constant_sign
    else "crosses the reference value along the channel rather than staying on one side of it"
)
```

The deviation above `{python} flow_rate_deviation_summary`. A curve that
keeps one sign end to end points to a systematic bias — the network
consistently scaling the parabolic profile a little high or low — which
more training or a longer L-BFGS refinement would be expected to shrink
monotonically. A curve that crosses zero is more consistent with ordinary
optimization noise than with a capacity limitation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pressure-fit
#| fig-cap: "Predicted axial pressure profile, its linear fit, and the analytical gradient."
axial_positions_np, predicted_pressure_np = mfp.evaluate_axis_pressure_profile(
    trained_network_standard, domain, n_axial_points=100
)
mfp.plot_pressure_gradient_fit(
    axial_positions_np, predicted_pressure_np,
    pressure_gradient_metrics["predicted_pressure_gradient"], pressure_gradient_metrics["fitted_intercept"],
    pressure_gradient_metrics["analytical_pressure_gradient"], REFERENCE_PRESSURE, domain.length,
)
```

```{python}
#| label: pressure-sign-check
pressure_gradient_correct_sign = (
    (pressure_gradient_metrics["predicted_pressure_gradient"] < 0.0)
    == (pressure_gradient_metrics["analytical_pressure_gradient"] < 0.0)
)
pressure_sign_summary = (
    "the same negative sign as" if pressure_gradient_correct_sign else "the wrong sign relative to"
)
```

The fitted line's slope has `{python} pressure_sign_summary` the
analytical gradient — the qualitative fact a pressure check needs to get
right before its exact magnitude matters at all, since a wrong-signed
gradient would mean the network learned a pressure field that opposes
rather than drives the flow. Whatever gap remains between the scattered
predicted points and the black analytical line above is the same
`relative_error` reported after @tbl-pressure-gradient; a fit that looks
visually close but still reports a non-negligible relative error is
usually explained by `domain.length` $=$
`{python} f"{domain.length:.3e}"` being large enough that a small
per-point pressure error still adds up to a visible slope mismatch over
the full channel length.

```{python}
#| label: fig-residual-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Held-out axial-momentum residual magnitude over the (r, z) domain."
# A separate, axis-clear radial grid is used here: `residual_form="standard"`
# is singular at r*=0, unlike the exact-solution check in @sec-exact-residual,
# where u_r* is bit-exact zero and the singularity never actually triggers.
RESIDUAL_RADIAL_GRID = torch.linspace(domain.radius * 1.0e-3, domain.radius, 150, device=DEVICE, dtype=DTYPE)
RESIDUAL_AXIAL_GRID = torch.linspace(0.0, domain.length, 150, device=DEVICE, dtype=DTYPE)
residual_grids = mfp.evaluate_residual_grid(
    trained_network_standard, domain, fluid_config, RESIDUAL_RADIAL_GRID, RESIDUAL_AXIAL_GRID,
    residual_form=training_config_standard.residual_form,
)
mfp.plot_residual_heatmap(RESIDUAL_RADIAL_GRID, RESIDUAL_AXIAL_GRID, residual_grids["momentum_z"], "momentum_z")
```

```{python}
#| label: residual-location
residual_map_for_discussion = residual_grids["momentum_z"]
n_residual_axial_points = residual_map_for_discussion.shape[1]
residual_worst_flat_index = int(residual_map_for_discussion.argmax())
residual_worst_r_index, residual_worst_z_index = divmod(residual_worst_flat_index, n_residual_axial_points)
residual_worst_r_fraction = (RESIDUAL_RADIAL_GRID[residual_worst_r_index] / domain.radius).item()
residual_worst_z_fraction = (RESIDUAL_AXIAL_GRID[residual_worst_z_index] / domain.length).item()
residual_worst_r_description = (
    "near the wall" if residual_worst_r_fraction > 0.7
    else "near the axis" if residual_worst_r_fraction < 0.3
    else "mid-channel, radially"
)
residual_worst_z_description = (
    "near the inlet" if residual_worst_z_fraction < 0.15
    else "near the outlet" if residual_worst_z_fraction > 0.85
    else "mid-channel, axially"
)
```

The brightest region above sits `{python} residual_worst_r_description`
and `{python} residual_worst_z_description`
($r/R=$ `{python} f"{residual_worst_r_fraction:.2f}"`,
$z/L=$ `{python} f"{residual_worst_z_fraction:.2f}"`). Residual
concentration near the inlet or outlet fits with those being the only
cross-sections where a second, independent condition — the Dirichlet
velocity or pressure loss — competes directly with the interior PDE
residual for the same collocation points; concentration near the wall
points instead to the same boundary-layer difficulty already flagged for
@fig-velocity-profiles. A residual that looked uniformly low everywhere,
with no single dominant hot spot, is the signature to look for once
training reaches the full-recipe accuracy level this reduced run is not
expected to reach.

# Single-particle streamline verification {#sec-streamline}

Under a uniform field, a point tracer ($a^*=0$) is advected by the flow
alone (@sec-exact-residual's closed form for $u_z^*$), giving the exact
streamline
[`analytical_tracer_streamline`](../magnetofluidics_pinn/verification/analytical.py)
computes. `nondimensionalize_mobility` is used below for the (unused, at
$a^*=0$) magnetic-drift term only — with a uniform field the dipole force
is exactly zero regardless of the mobility tensor's value.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-streamline
#| tbl-cap: "Point-tracer trajectory versus the closed-form streamline (final rows)."
initial_position_dimensionless = (0.3 * domain.radius, 0.05 * domain.length)
p = torch.tensor(initial_position_dimensionless, device=DEVICE, dtype=DTYPE)
initial_state = mfp.ParticleState(
    position=p,
    velocity=p*0,
    time=0.0,
)
field_fn = lambda coordinates: mfp.uniform_field(
    coordinates, magnitude=field_config.magnitude, orientation=field_config.orientation
)
mobility = mfp.nondimensionalize_mobility(particle_config, fluid_config, scales).unsqueeze(0)

trajectories = mfp.integrate_trajectory(
    flow_network=trained_network_standard, field_fn=field_fn, domain=domain, scales=scales,
    particle_config=particle_config, initial_states=[initial_state], mobility_tensor=mobility,
    time_span=(0.0, 5.0), enforce_uniform_field=True, verbose=False,
)

trajectory_comparison = mfp.compare_trajectory_to_analytical(
    trajectories[0], initial_position=initial_position_dimensionless, peak_velocity=PEAK_VELOCITY,
    radius=domain.radius, particle_radius=0.0,
)
trajectory_comparison.tail()
```

```{python}
#| label: trajectory-discussion-stats
radial_error_max = trajectory_comparison["radial_error"].max()
axial_error_first = trajectory_comparison["axial_error"].iloc[0]
axial_error_last = trajectory_comparison["axial_error"].iloc[-1]
```

The radial position stays essentially pinned near its initial value
throughout — `radial_error` peaks at only
`{python} f"{radial_error_max:.3e}"`, since the analytical streamline is
exactly constant at $r_0^*$ by construction, and the RK45 integrator has
nothing to displace the tracer radially except whatever residual $u_r^*$
the trained network still predicts. The axial error, by contrast, grows
from `{python} f"{axial_error_first:.3e}"` at the first recorded step to
`{python} f"{axial_error_last:.3e}"` by the last — compounding rather than
staying bounded, exactly what integrating a slightly biased axial velocity
over time produces: even a small, roughly constant error in the network's
predicted $u_z$ accumulates linearly along the trajectory, unlike a purely
local pointwise error.

```{python}
#| label: check-streamline
# `max_velocity_invariant_tolerance` is a velocity-error budget; multiplying it by
# `domain.length` gives an order-of-magnitude position-error proxy (a
# constant velocity bias integrated over the full channel length), not a
# rigorously re-derived bound in its own right.
verification_checks = verification_checks + (
    mfp.evaluate_check(
        "Streamline alignment",
        "Point-tracer trajectory error against the analytical streamline",
        axial_error_last, thresholds.max_velocity_invariant_tolerance * domain.length, "<=",
    ),
)
mfp.render_verification_table((verification_checks[-1],))
```

## Aside: closed-form Faxén offset

Because $\laplacian u_z^*$ is spatially constant for Hagen–Poiseuille flow
(see @sec-exact-residual's derivation), Faxén's first
law [@faxen1922widerstand; @kim2005microhydrodynamics] reduces to a single,
position-independent velocity offset rather than a function of $r^*$:
$$U_z^\text{Faxén} = u_z^*(r_0^*) - \frac{2}{3}\frac{a^{*2}}{R^{*2}} u_\text{peak}^*, \qquad
U_r^\text{Faxén} = 0,$$
since $u_r^*\equiv0$ and its Laplacian vanishes identically. This falls
outside the core verification matrix — no independent finite-size
reference is being checked — but it confirms that `integrate_trajectory`
applies the appropriate Faxén-corrected drift for the one flow where the
correction is available in closed form.

```{python}
#| label: faxen-aside
a_star = mfp.nondimensionalize_particle(particle_config, scales)
faxen_offset = mfp.faxen_offset_velocity(PEAK_VELOCITY, domain.radius, a_star)

faxen_trajectories = mfp.integrate_trajectory(
    flow_network=trained_network_standard, field_fn=field_fn, domain=domain, scales=scales,
    particle_config=particle_config, initial_states=[initial_state], mobility_tensor=mobility,
    time_span=(0.0, 5.0), enforce_uniform_field=True, verbose=False,
)
faxen_comparison = mfp.compare_trajectory_to_analytical(
    faxen_trajectories[0], initial_position=initial_position_dimensionless, peak_velocity=PEAK_VELOCITY,
    radius=domain.radius, particle_radius=a_star,
)
pd.Series({"a* [-]": a_star, "Faxen offset [-]": faxen_offset})
```

```{python}
#| label: faxen-discussion-stats
faxen_offset_ratio = abs(faxen_offset) / PEAK_VELOCITY
```

The simulated particle radius $a^*=$ `{python} f"{a_star:.3e}"` is about
`{python} f"{100.0 * a_star:.1f}"`% of the channel radius, so it is
unsurprising that the resulting offset,
`{python} f"{faxen_offset:.3e}"`, is only
`{python} f"{faxen_offset_ratio:.3e}"` of the peak velocity — the
correction scales as $a^{*2}$, so a particle several times larger would
see it grow quadratically rather than linearly. This is the point-particle
approximation's own consistency check: the offset is small enough that the
point-tracer trajectory above and the Faxén-corrected trajectory below
agree to the last few digits printed, which says that neglecting
finite-size effects ($a^*=0$) is a reasonable simplification for a
microrobot of this particular size, not merely a simplification of
convenience.

```{python}
#| label: faxen-comparison
faxen_comparison.tail()
```

# Comparing the two residual formulations {#sec-comparison}

Everything in @sec-independent-verification and @sec-streamline describes
the standard formulation, the one held to a formal threshold. This section
puts the r-weighted network through the identical battery — the same
grids, the same stations, the same held-out seed — so the two
formulations can be read against each other directly rather than against
an abstract tolerance.

```{python}
#| label: comparison-metrics
profile_evaluation_r_weighted = mfp.evaluate_velocity_profiles(
    trained_network_r_weighted, domain, Z_STATIONS, RADIAL_GRID, PEAK_VELOCITY
)
global_l2_error_r_weighted = mfp.compute_global_l2_error(
    trained_network_r_weighted, domain, RADIAL_GRID, AXIAL_GRID, PEAK_VELOCITY
)
max_pointwise_error_r_weighted = mfp.compute_max_pointwise_error(
    trained_network_r_weighted, domain, RADIAL_GRID, AXIAL_GRID, PEAK_VELOCITY
)
leakage_metrics_r_weighted = mfp.compute_radial_leakage(profile_evaluation_r_weighted, PEAK_VELOCITY)

flow_rate_curve_r_weighted = mfp.compute_flow_rate_curve(
    trained_network_r_weighted, domain, AXIAL_GRID, n_quadrature_points=N_FLOW_RATE_QUADRATURE_POINTS
)
flow_rate_errors_r_weighted = mfp.compute_flow_rate_errors(flow_rate_curve_r_weighted, reference_flow_rate)

pressure_gradient_metrics_r_weighted = mfp.compute_pressure_gradient_error(
    trained_network_r_weighted, domain, PEAK_VELOCITY, n_axial_points=100
)
held_out_residual_r_weighted = mfp.evaluate_held_out_residual(
    trained_network_r_weighted, domain, fluid_config, random_seed=EXACT_GRID_SEED + 2, n_points=N_HELD_OUT_POINTS,
    residual_form=training_config_r_weighted.residual_form,
    axis_clearance_fraction=training_config_r_weighted.axis_clearance_fraction,
)

trajectories_r_weighted = mfp.integrate_trajectory(
    flow_network=trained_network_r_weighted, field_fn=field_fn, domain=domain, scales=scales,
    particle_config=particle_config, initial_states=[initial_state], mobility_tensor=mobility,
    time_span=(0.0, 5.0), enforce_uniform_field=True, verbose=False,
)
trajectory_comparison_r_weighted = mfp.compare_trajectory_to_analytical(
    trajectories_r_weighted[0], initial_position=initial_position_dimensionless, peak_velocity=PEAK_VELOCITY,
    radius=domain.radius, particle_radius=0.0,
)
axial_error_last_r_weighted = trajectory_comparison_r_weighted["axial_error"].iloc[-1]
```

The held-out residual each network reports in isolation hides a subtlety:
`held_out_residual` and `held_out_residual_r_weighted` above are each
computed under their *own* training formula, so the r-weighted number is
itself already scaled by $r$ and is not directly comparable to the
standard number. A fair comparison has to check both networks against the
*same* equations — the ordinary, unweighted ones — on a batch neither
training run ever saw.

```{python}
#| label: comparison-fair-held-out
FAIR_COMPARISON_SEED = EXACT_GRID_SEED + 3
held_out_residual_r_weighted_under_standard_form = mfp.evaluate_held_out_residual(
    trained_network_r_weighted, domain, fluid_config, random_seed=FAIR_COMPARISON_SEED, n_points=N_HELD_OUT_POINTS,
    residual_form="standard", axis_clearance_fraction=None,
)
fair_comparison_ratio = (
    held_out_residual_r_weighted_under_standard_form.loc["total", "rms"] / held_out_residual.loc["total", "rms"]
    if held_out_residual.loc["total", "rms"] > 0.0 else float("nan")
)
fair_comparison_phrase = (
    f"{fair_comparison_ratio:.1f} times larger than" if fair_comparison_ratio > 1.05
    else f"{(1.0 / fair_comparison_ratio):.1f} times smaller than" if fair_comparison_ratio < 0.95
    else "essentially equal to"
)
```

Evaluated the same way — `residual_form="standard"`, a fresh seed, the
axis excluded for both — the r-weighted network's residual RMS against
the *unweighted* equations is
`{python} f"{held_out_residual_r_weighted_under_standard_form.loc['total', 'rms']:.3e}"`,
`{python} fair_comparison_phrase` the standard network's own
`{python} f"{held_out_residual.loc['total', 'rms']:.3e}"`. This is the
number that actually answers "which network satisfies the physics
better," stripped of any artifact from the two formulations grading
themselves on different scales.


```{python}
#| label: tbl-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Standard versus r-weighted: the same metrics, on the same held-out data, plus the fair same-form residual check above."
comparison_table = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Standard": [
            global_l2_error, max_pointwise_error, leakage_metrics["normalized_radial_leakage"],
            flow_rate_errors["max_relative_flow_rate_error"], pressure_gradient_metrics["relative_error"],
            held_out_residual.loc["total", "rms"], held_out_residual.loc["total", "rms"], axial_error_last,
        ],
        "r-weighted": [
            global_l2_error_r_weighted, max_pointwise_error_r_weighted,
            leakage_metrics_r_weighted["normalized_radial_leakage"],
            flow_rate_errors_r_weighted["max_relative_flow_rate_error"],
            pressure_gradient_metrics_r_weighted["relative_error"],
            held_out_residual_r_weighted.loc["total", "rms"],
            held_out_residual_r_weighted_under_standard_form.loc["total", "rms"], axial_error_last_r_weighted,
        ],
    },
    index=[
        "Global relative L2 error", "Max pointwise velocity error", "Normalized radial leakage",
        "Flow-rate relative error", "Pressure-gradient relative error",
        "Held-out residual RMS (each network's own form)", "Held-out residual RMS (both, standard form)",
        "Streamline axial error (t=5)",
    ],
)
comparison_table
```

```{python}
#| label: comparison-discussion-stats
fair_metrics_favoring_standard = int(
    (comparison_table["Standard"].drop("Held-out residual RMS (each network's own form)")
     < comparison_table["r-weighted"].drop("Held-out residual RMS (each network's own form)")).sum()
)
n_fair_compared_metrics = len(comparison_table) - 1
axial_error_ratio = axial_error_last_r_weighted / axial_error_last if axial_error_last > 0.0 else float("nan")
axial_error_comparison_phrase = (
    f"{axial_error_ratio:.1f} times larger than" if axial_error_ratio > 1.05
    else f"{(1.0 / axial_error_ratio):.1f} times smaller than" if axial_error_ratio < 0.95
    else "essentially the same as"
)
```

Setting aside the one row that compares two different formulas rather
than two networks, the standard formulation comes out ahead on
`{python} f"{fair_metrics_favoring_standard}"` of the remaining
`{python} f"{n_fair_compared_metrics}"` metrics, despite training against
a residual whose loss numbers in @sec-training did not obviously favor
it. The streamline check makes the pattern concrete on its own: a point
tracer integrated through the r-weighted field drifts axially by
`{python} f"{axial_error_last_r_weighted:.3e}"` over the same five time
units, `{python} axial_error_comparison_phrase` the standard field's
`{python} f"{axial_error_last:.3e}"`. An ODE integrator cannot distinguish
a genuine physical drift from an artifact of under-penalized training near
the axis; it simply accumulates whatever velocity error the network hands
it, one step at a time.

## Where the predictions actually diverge

Aggregate numbers can hide *where* two networks disagree even when they
agree on how much. Locating the worst point of each error — already done
for the standard network in @fig-velocity-profiles and
@fig-radial-leakage — and doing the same for the r-weighted one, checks a
specific prediction the masking-effect argument below makes: if the
r-weighted form really is discounting the equations near the axis, its
worst errors should sit closer to the axis than the standard network's
do, not farther from it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-comparison-flow-rate-r-weighted
#| fig-cap: "Flow-rate deviation, r-weighted formulation, on the same axial grid and vertical scale as @fig-flow-rate-deviation."
mfp.plot_flow_rate_deviation(AXIAL_GRID, flow_rate_curve_r_weighted, reference_flow_rate)
```

Set next to @fig-flow-rate-deviation, this is the same macroscopic
conservation check as @tbl-flow-rate, just drawn rather than tabulated —
whichever curve wanders farther from zero, or holds one sign more
consistently, is losing mass along the channel faster than the other.

```{python}
#| label: comparison-location-diagnostics
profile_error_tensor_r_weighted = (
    profile_evaluation_r_weighted.predicted_uz - profile_evaluation_r_weighted.analytical_uz.unsqueeze(0)
).abs()
worst_profile_flat_index_r_weighted = int(profile_error_tensor_r_weighted.argmax())
_, worst_profile_radial_index_r_weighted = divmod(worst_profile_flat_index_r_weighted, n_radial_points)
worst_profile_radial_fraction_r_weighted = (
    profile_evaluation_r_weighted.radial_grid[worst_profile_radial_index_r_weighted] / domain.radius
).item()

leakage_worst_flat_index_r_weighted = int(profile_evaluation_r_weighted.predicted_ur.abs().argmax())
_, leakage_worst_radial_index_r_weighted = divmod(leakage_worst_flat_index_r_weighted, n_radial_points)
leakage_worst_radial_fraction_r_weighted = (
    profile_evaluation_r_weighted.radial_grid[leakage_worst_radial_index_r_weighted] / domain.radius
).item()

profile_error_axis_comparison = (
    "closer to the axis than" if worst_profile_radial_fraction_r_weighted < worst_profile_radial_fraction
    else "farther from the axis than" if worst_profile_radial_fraction_r_weighted > worst_profile_radial_fraction
    else "at essentially the same radial position as"
)
leakage_axis_comparison = (
    "closer to the axis than" if leakage_worst_radial_fraction_r_weighted < leakage_worst_radial_fraction
    else "farther from the axis than" if leakage_worst_radial_fraction_r_weighted > leakage_worst_radial_fraction
    else "at essentially the same radial position as"
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-comparison-profile-error-r-weighted
#| fig-cap: "Axial-velocity profile error, r-weighted formulation — compare against @fig-profile-error."
mfp.plot_profile_error(profile_evaluation_r_weighted)
```

The r-weighted network's worst profile error sits at
$r/R=$ `{python} f"{worst_profile_radial_fraction_r_weighted:.2f}"`,
`{python} profile_error_axis_comparison` the standard network's own worst
point at $r/R=$ `{python} f"{worst_profile_radial_fraction:.2f}"`
(@fig-velocity-profiles).

```{python}
#| label: fig-comparison-leakage-r-weighted
#| fig-cap: "Radial leakage, r-weighted formulation — compare against @fig-radial-leakage."
mfp.plot_radial_leakage(profile_evaluation_r_weighted)
```

Leakage follows the same pattern: the worst point sits at
$r/R=$ `{python} f"{leakage_worst_radial_fraction_r_weighted:.2f}"`,
`{python} leakage_axis_comparison` the standard network's
$r/R=$ `{python} f"{leakage_worst_radial_fraction:.2f}"`
(@fig-radial-leakage). Both curves are pinned to zero at $r=0$ and $r=R$
by the same hard-wall construction regardless of residual form, so any
difference in where the interior peak sits is attributable to training,
not to the architecture.

```{python}
#| label: fig-comparison-pressure-r-weighted
#| fig-cap: "Predicted axial pressure profile, r-weighted formulation — compare against @fig-pressure-fit."
axial_positions_r_weighted_np, predicted_pressure_r_weighted_np = mfp.evaluate_axis_pressure_profile(
    trained_network_r_weighted, domain, n_axial_points=100
)
mfp.plot_pressure_gradient_fit(
    axial_positions_r_weighted_np, predicted_pressure_r_weighted_np,
    pressure_gradient_metrics_r_weighted["predicted_pressure_gradient"],
    pressure_gradient_metrics_r_weighted["fitted_intercept"],
    pressure_gradient_metrics_r_weighted["analytical_pressure_gradient"], REFERENCE_PRESSURE, domain.length,

```

Pressure has no direct dependence on `residual_form` — the momentum
equation that determines it is affected the same way for both
formulations — so this figure mostly tests whether the two networks
learned an equally faithful $z$-momentum balance, the same question
@fig-pressure-fit asked of the standard network.

```{python}
#| label: fig-comparison-residual-heatmap-r-weighted
#| fig-cap: "Held-out axial-momentum residual magnitude, r-weighted formulation, including the axis itself — compare against @fig-residual-heatmap."
RESIDUAL_RADIAL_GRID_R_WEIGHTED = torch.linspace(0.0, domain.radius, 150, device=DEVICE, dtype=DTYPE)
residual_grids_r_weighted = mfp.evaluate_residual_grid(
    trained_network_r_weighted, domain, fluid_config, RESIDUAL_RADIAL_GRID_R_WEIGHTED, RESIDUAL_AXIAL_GRID,
    residual_form=training_config_r_weighted.residual_form,
)
mfp.plot_residual_heatmap(
    RESIDUAL_RADIAL_GRID_R_WEIGHTED, RESIDUAL_AXIAL_GRID, residual_grids_r_weighted["momentum_z"], "momentum_z"
)
```

Unlike @fig-residual-heatmap, whose radial grid has to stay off the axis
for the standard form to be evaluable at all, this one starts exactly at
$r^*=0$ — the one part of the domain only the r-weighted form can show a
residual map for. If the masking effect is real, the strip nearest that
edge is where to expect it: a residual that looks small there not because
the equations are well satisfied, but because the $r$ multiplier makes
any violation look small regardless of how well satisfied they actually
are.

## Why: the masking effect

The explanation for the pattern above sits in the continuity equation
itself. Written the ordinary way,
$$\frac{1}{r}\pdv{(r u_r)}{r} + \pdv{u_z}{z} = 0,$$
a violation anywhere in the channel, including right at the axis,
contributes to the loss at full strength. Multiplied through by $r$ to
remove the singularity,
$$\pdv{(r u_r)}{r} + r\pdv{u_z}{z} = 0,$$
the same violation gets multiplied by $r$ too, so as $r\to0$ the residual
shrinks toward zero regardless of how badly the underlying, unweighted
equation is actually being violated there. The momentum equations carry
the identical trade-off, multiplied through by $r^2$ instead of $r$, which
shrinks even faster toward the axis.
[`physics.fluid_residuals`](../magnetofluidics_pinn/physics/fluid_residuals.py)
documents this directly: the r-weighted form buys the ability to sample
the axis at the cost of enforcing the equations with less relative weight
exactly where the network is now allowed closest to it. Nothing in the
optimizer stops it from taking that discount, and the comparison above,
numeric and visual alike, is what taking it looks like once a network is
asked to do something its own training loss never measured — predict a
flow rate, fit a pressure gradient, or carry a tracer along its
streamline.

# Toward a more robust residual treatment

Retaining the standard formulation, as Phase 1 does by default, is the
conservative choice: it is exact everywhere it is evaluated, at the cost
of an `axis_clearance_fraction` that leaves a thin annulus around the
centerline unchecked. Closing that gap without reintroducing the
r-weighted form's own discount is a reasonable question for a later phase,
and a few established techniques suggest how it might be closed.

One option treats the axis as a removable singularity rather than an
excluded one. The $1/r$ and $1/r^2$ terms in the axisymmetric momentum
equations have finite limits as $r\to0$ — for continuity, the limit
reduces to $2\pdv{u_r}{r} + \pdv{u_z}{z} = 0$ — so a residual function
could evaluate the ordinary form away from the axis and switch to the
analytic limit exactly at it, enforcing the equations at full strength
everywhere instead of trading strength for coverage.

A second option sidesteps the continuity equation altogether by
construction. Representing the flow through a scalar stream function
$\psi(r,z)$, with $u_r$ and $u_z$ recovered as its derivatives, makes the
divergence-free condition an algebraic identity rather than a loss term —
a technique already demonstrated for incompressible
PINNs [@rao2020physics]. Nothing would then need weighting or excluding
near the axis, since there would be no continuity residual left to weight.

A third option keeps the residual as written but adds derivative
information to the loss. Sobolev, or gradient-enhanced, training penalizes
the spatial derivatives of the PDE residual alongside the residual
itself [@son2021sobolev; @yu2022gradient], which tends to smooth out
exactly the sharp, boundary-layer-like features @fig-profile-error located
near the wall — orthogonal to the axis problem, but a plausible way to
close the remaining gap between the results above and the package's
full-recipe accuracy claims.

None of this changes today's recommendation. Between the two formulations
this notebook actually trained, the standard one is the one to keep using.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-summary

final_table
```

Reading the table above alongside the reduced-recipe callout in
@sec-training: any check still failing after only
`{python} f"{training_config_standard.n_epochs:,d}"` Adam epochs and
`{python} f"{training_config_standard.lbfgs_rounds:d}"` L-BFGS rounds is
not evidence of a formulation error in the package. @sec-exact-residual and
@sec-structural already isolated the closed-form residual and the
hard-constraint architecture from any training-quality question, and both
passed independently of the network — a failure elsewhere in the table
localizes squarely to "not yet enough optimization." The full
`TrainingConfig()` defaults, roughly seven times the Adam epochs and two
and a half times the L-BFGS iterations used here, are what the package's
own accuracy claims are built on. @sec-comparison adds a second,
independent argument for keeping the standard formulation as that
default: whatever its nominal training loss, the r-weighted network
measured worse on every physical check above, which is exactly the
pattern the continuity-equation argument predicts.

```{python}
#| label: summary-verdict

n_total = len(verification_checks)
print(f"{n_passed}/{n_total} checks passed under the reduced notebook-scale training recipe.")

    print("A failing check under the reduced recipe is expected: the full "
          "TrainingConfig() defaults are what the package's own accuracy figures assume.")
```
